lesson.title: Six Points, Perfect Symmetry: The Octahedral Shape
lesson.summary: Octahedral geometry places six electron domains at the six equivalent corners of a highly symmetric solid, giving molecules like sulfur hexafluoride uniform 90 degree angles and remarkable structural simplicity.
lesson.body:
A steric number of six pushes VSEPR theory to its most symmetric result. Six electron domains around a central atom require twelve electrons total, well beyond the standard octet, so octahedral geometry, like trigonal bipyramidal geometry, only forms around period three and larger elements capable of an expanded octet. What makes octahedral geometry distinctive compared to trigonal bipyramidal geometry is that all six positions turn out to be completely equivalent to one another, with no separate axial and equatorial categories to keep track of.

The shape itself, called an octahedron, has six vertices and eight triangular faces, which is where its name comes from. Picture two square pyramids joined together at their square bases: the six points where a central atom's domains sit are the four corners of that shared square base plus the two apex points above and below it. Every pair of adjacent domains sits 90 degrees apart, and every pair of domains directly across from each other sits 180 degrees apart. Because every one of the six positions is geometrically identical to every other position, unlike the axial and equatorial split seen in trigonal bipyramidal geometry, octahedral geometry is considered the more symmetric of the two expanded octet shapes.

Sulfur hexafluoride, SF6, is the standard example of an ideal octahedral molecule. Sulfur, a period three element, forms six single bonds to six fluorine atoms and retains no lone pairs, using all six available domains as bonding pairs. With a steric number of six and zero lone pairs, both the electron geometry and the molecular geometry are octahedral, and because all six substituents are identical fluorine atoms, every F to S to F angle between adjacent fluorines measures exactly 90 degrees, while opposite fluorines sit at 180 degrees. All six S to F bonds are fully equivalent by symmetry.

Sulfur hexafluoride's structure is not just a geometry exercise, it has real consequences for the molecule's behavior. The six fluorine atoms surrounding sulfur so symmetrically and so completely shield the central sulfur atom that SF6 is remarkably unreactive and thermally stable, which is why it is used as an electrical insulating gas in high voltage equipment. The tight, symmetric packing that VSEPR predicts translates directly into a real, measurable chemical property.

Just as trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry gives rise to other molecular shapes once lone pairs replace some of its bonding domains, octahedral electron geometry does the same. A central atom with six total domains but one lone pair produces a square pyramidal molecular shape, and one with six total domains and two lone pairs produces a square planar shape, since the two lone pairs settle into the geometrically most stable positions directly across from one another. Both of these are direct extensions of the same octahedral framework covered here, applying the same core VSEPR logic of minimizing repulsion that has driven every geometry discussed so far.
